Uncle Bob Martin just ran an experiment that should worry everyone building AI agent systems.

If you don't know the name, here's why it matters.

Robert C. Martin wrote Clean Code, the book that shaped how a whole generation of developers thinks about software quality. He was one of the original signatories of the Agile Manifesto in 2001. He's the guy who popularized the SOLID principles most engineers learn in their first year on the job.

He's been writing software for over 50 years.

So when people argue about whether AI coding is real engineering or a shortcut, his opinion carries weight that most voices in the vibe coding debate don't have. He built his career on the structure of software, not on the hype around it.

And he just posted a video saying his structure might be the problem.

For months he built a harness, a system that coordinates multiple AI agents on one task. It had agents handing off work to each other, deterministic tools for each one, and tight quality constraints. It was the classic software engineering approach applied to AI.

Then he gave the same task to a single Grok agent with one plain prompt and walked away.

The single agent finished in 40 minutes. The harness took 3 to 4 hours. The single agent's output was better.

He even loosened his code quality target for the solo run, and the agent came in under his original stricter target anyway. Nobody told it to.

His conclusion is that agents might not belong in a software design as components at all. The models got good enough that the scaffolding around them is now the thing doing the damage.

I put the full comparison in the infographic below. Save it, because this is the argument you'll be having with your team next quarter.
